title: The Sun Is About to Disappear Over Europe—Here's How to Watch!
summary: Imagine the middle of the day suddenly turning into night. The sky darkens, stars pop out, and the air gets chilly. That's what happens during a total solar eclipse—and one is coming to Europe on August 12! A solar eclipse happens when the Moon moves right between Earth and the Sun, blocking the Sun's light. For a short time, a narrow path on Earth is plunged into darkness. In that path, you can see the Sun's thin, wispy outer atmosphere, called the corona, glowing around the Moon. Birds might even start acting like it's bedtime! This eclipse's path of totality—where the Moon completely covers the Sun—will cross Greenland, Iceland, a tiny bit of Portugal, and Spain. If you're not in those places, don't worry! The European Space Agency (ESA) is broadcasting the whole thing live from a special observatory in Spain called Javalambre. The show starts at 1:30 p.m. EDT on ESA Web TV or YouTube. At 2:31 p.m. EDT, the Moon will fully cover the Sun for 1 minute and 21 seconds at the observatory. Telescopes and drones will capture every moment. Scientists will explain cool stuff like how an eclipse once helped prove Einstein's ideas about gravity. Even if you're far away, you can watch the Sun vanish and reappear from your screen!
why_it_matters: Even if you can't see the eclipse in the sky, watching a live broadcast lets you experience one of nature's rarest shows and learn how scientists discovered secrets of the universe.

background_read: Solar eclipses don't happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted, so the Moon, Sun, and Earth have to line up just right.
The last total solar eclipse visible in parts of Europe was in 1999, and the next one after 2025 will be in 2026, passing over parts of Greenland and Iceland again.
Einstein's 1915 theory of general relativity said gravity could bend starlight, and a total solar eclipse in 1919 let scientists photograph stars near the Sun to prove him right.
